hmmt-feb-2014-team-01.title: Center on segment $OA$
hmmt-feb-2014-team-01.body:
Let $O$ be the center and $R$ the radius of $\omega$, and assume $OA\ge OB$. Consider $g(P)=PA-PB$ for $P$ moving along segment $OA$ from $O$ to $A$. At $P=O$, $g=OA-OB\ge0$, and at $P=A$, $g=-AB<0$. By continuity there is a point $C$ on segment $OA$ with $CA=CB=:y$. Let $\omega'$ be the circle with center $C$ and radius $y$; it passes through $A$ and $B$.

Let $P$ be any point on or inside $\omega'$. Since $C$ lies on segment $OA$, $OC=OA-y$, so by the triangle inequality $OP\le OC+CP\le(OA-y)+y=OA<R$. Hence $P$ lies in the interior of $\omega$, and $\omega'$ is contained in the interior of $\omega$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2014-team-02.title: Group by $\gcd(a_i,210)$
hmmt-feb-2014-team-02.body:
Let $g_i=\gcd(a_i,210)$. Since $a_i\mid a_{i+1}$, $g_i\mid g_{i+1}$, so the sequence $g_i$ passes through a chain of divisors $1$-or-more of $210=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$ in which each step multiplies by some primes; at most $5$ distinct values occur, and a chain of five has the form $1,p_1,p_1p_2,p_1p_2p_3,210$ for some ordering $(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)$ of $(2,3,5,7)$ (shorter chains give no more terms). The remainders $b_i$ with $\gcd(b_i,210)=g$ number $\varphi(210/g)$ values. So the number of distinct $b_i$ is at most
$$\varphi(210)+\varphi\\!\left(\tfrac{210}{p_1}\right)+\varphi\\!\left(\tfrac{210}{p_1p_2}\right)+\varphi\\!\left(\tfrac{210}{p_1p_2p_3}\right)+1 .$$
To maximize, choose $p_1$ to maximize $\varphi(210/p_1)$: $\varphi(105)=48$ for $p_1=2$, versus $24,12,8$ for $3,5,7$. Then $\varphi(\frac{210}{2p_2})$ is largest for $p_2=3$ ($\varphi(35)=24$), then $p_3=5$ ($\varphi(7)=6$). The bound is $48+48+24+6+1=127$.

Attainability: let $a_i$ run through numbers coprime to $210$ that realize all $48$ units mod $210$ (successive terms multiplied by integers coprime to $210$ congruent to the needed ratio), then multiply by $2$ and realize all $48$ residues of the form $2u$, then by $3$ ($24$ residues), by $5$ ($6$), and finally by $7$ (the residue $0$). Each term divides the next.

**Answer: 127**

hmmt-feb-2014-team-03.title: Upper bound and construction
hmmt-feb-2014-team-03.body:
Model the problem as a bipartite graph with an edge for every suitable pair; we want to maximize the number of edges subject to there being a unique perfect matching.

*Construction:* join $G_i$ to $B_j$ for all $j\le i$. The only perfect matching is $G_i\leftrightarrow B_i$ for all $i$ (induct from $G_1$, whose only edge is to $B_1$, etc.). The number of edges is $1+2+\cdots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}2$.

*Bound:* relabel so that the unique matching is $G_i\leftrightarrow B_i$; this uses $n$ edges. For $i\ne j$, the edges $G_iB_j$ and $G_jB_i$ cannot both be present, otherwise swapping gives a second perfect matching (pair $G_i$ with $B_j$, $G_j$ with $B_i$, others unchanged). So among the $\binom n2$ unordered pairs $\{i,j\}$ at most one extra edge each: at most $n+\binom n2=\frac{n(n+1)}2$ edges.

**Answer: $\frac{n(n+1)}2$**

hmmt-feb-2014-team-04.title: Pair $k$ with $100-k$
hmmt-feb-2014-team-04.body:
Let $a_k=\frac{2^{100}}{2^{50}+2^k}$. For $0\le k\le100$: $a_{100-k}=\frac{2^{100}}{2^{50}+2^{100-k}}=\frac{2^{50+k}}{2^k+2^{50}}$, so $a_k+a_{100-k}=\frac{2^{100}+2^{50+k}}{2^{50}+2^k}=2^{50}$.

For $0\le k\le49$, $a_k$ is not an integer (its denominator is $2^k(2^{50-k}+1)$ with an odd factor larger than $1$ not dividing $2^{100}$), and then neither is $a_{100-k}=2^{50}-a_k$. Hence $\lfloor a_k\rfloor+\lfloor a_{100-k}\rfloor=2^{50}-1$ (the floors of two non-integers summing to an integer sum to that integer minus $1$). The middle term is $a_{50}=\frac{2^{100}}{2^{51}}=2^{49}$.

Total: $50(2^{50}-1)+2^{49}=100\cdot2^{49}+2^{49}-50=101\cdot2^{49}-50$.

**Answer: $101\cdot2^{49}-50$**

hmmt-feb-2014-team-05.title: The image is a hyperbola with a focus at 0
hmmt-feb-2014-team-05.body:
Write $z=e^{it}$. Then $1+z+z^2=z(z^{-1}+1+z)=z(1+2\cos t)$, so $w=\frac1{1+z+z^2}=\frac{\cos t-i\sin t}{1+2\cos t}=x+iy$ with $x=\frac{\cos t}{1+2\cos t}$, $y=\frac{-\sin t}{1+2\cos t}$ (note $1+2\cos t\ne0$).

Then $x-\frac23=\frac{3\cos t-2-4\cos t}{3(1+2\cos t)}=-\frac{2+\cos t}{3(1+2\cos t)}$, so
$$9\left(x-\tfrac23\right)^2-3y^2=\frac{(2+\cos t)^2-3\sin^2t}{(1+2\cos t)^2}=\frac{1+4\cos t+4\cos^2t}{(1+2\cos t)^2}=1 .$$
So $w$ lies on the hyperbola $\frac{(x-2/3)^2}{1/9}-\frac{y^2}{1/3}=1$, with center $\left(\frac23,0\right)$, $a=\frac13$, $b^2=\frac13$, focal distance $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\frac23$. Its foci are $0$ and $\frac43$. For every point $w$ of a hyperbola the difference of the distances to the foci has absolute value $2a$, so with $c=\frac43$,
$$\big||w|-|w-c|\big|=2a=\frac23=d$$
for all admissible $z$. ∎

**Answer: $c=\frac43$, $d=\frac23$**

hmmt-feb-2014-team-06.title: Generalize to $3b_i\le b_{i+1}$
hmmt-feb-2014-team-06.body:
**Claim.** Let $b_1<\cdots<b_n$ be positive integers with $3b_i\le b_{i+1}$. The number of sequences $(a_0,\dots,a_n)$ with $0=|a_0|<|a_1|<\cdots<|a_n|$ and $\{|a_k-a_{k-1}|\}=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ is $(n+1)!$. The problem is the case $b_i=3^{i-1}$.

**Lemma.** $b_i>2\sum_{k<i}b_k$. Indeed $\sum_{k<i}b_k\le b_i\left(\frac13+\frac19+\cdots+\frac1{3^{i-1}}\right)<\frac{b_i}2$.

**Induction.** $n=1$: $a_1=\pm b_1$, so $2=2!$ sequences. Suppose the claim holds for fewer than $j$ differences and consider $b_1<\cdots<b_j$. A sequence determines the order $c_1,\dots,c_j$ (a permutation of the $b$'s) in which the differences $|a_k-a_{k-1}|$ occur; let $c_k=b_j$.

- The first $k-1$ steps form an acceptable sequence for the set $\{c_1,\dots,c_{k-1}\}$ (which again satisfies $3b\le b'$ for consecutive elements); by induction there are $k!$ of them (for $k=1$ there is $1=1!$).
- By the lemma, $b_j>2\sum_{m<k}c_m\ge2|a_{k-1}|$, so both $a_k=a_{k-1}\pm b_j$ satisfy $|a_k|\ge b_j-|a_{k-1}|>|a_{k-1}|$: $2$ choices, and $|a_k|>\frac{b_j}2$.
- Afterwards, for each remaining step with difference $c\le b_j$, we have $|a_{i-1}|\ge|a_k|>\frac{b_j}2\ge\frac c2$. Moving $a_{i-1}\to a_{i-1}\pm c$ in the direction away from $0$ increases the absolute value; in the direction toward $0$ it gives $|\,|a_{i-1}|-c\,|<|a_{i-1}|$ (because $c<2|a_{i-1}|$). So exactly one sign works at each step.

Count: choose which $k-1$ of the other $j-1$ numbers are used before $b_j$ ($\binom{j-1}{k-1}$ ways), then $k!$ sequences for them, $2$ choices for $a_k$, and $(j-k)!$ orders for the rest (each giving exactly one sequence):
$$\sum_{k=1}^j\binom{j-1}{k-1}\\,k!\cdot2\cdot(j-k)!=\sum_{k=1}^j2(j-1)!\\,k=2(j-1)!\cdot\frac{j(j+1)}2=(j+1)!.$$
This completes the induction. ∎

hmmt-feb-2014-team-07.title: Construction and an upper bound
hmmt-feb-2014-team-07.body:
**$7$ is possible.** Take $A(0,0)$, $B\left(\frac12,1-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$, $C\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$, $D(0,1)$, $E\left(-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$, $F\left(-\frac12,1-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$. This hexagon is convex and the seven diagonals $AC,AD,AE,BD,BF,CE,DF$ all have length $1$ (only $BE$ and $CF$, of length about $1.24$, differ).

**$8$ is impossible.** Suppose at least $8$ of the $9$ diagonals have the same length; then removing one diagonal leaves $8$ equal ones. Up to relabeling, the removed diagonal is a short one ($AC$, say) or a long one ($AD$, say). In both cases $EC,EB,FB,FC$ are among the remaining equal diagonals. From $EB=FB$ and $EC=FC$, both $B$ and $C$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $EF$. Since the hexagon is convex, $B$ and $C$ lie on the same side of line $EF$ (it contains the side $EF$), so on this perpendicular bisector one of them lies inside the triangle formed by $E$, $F$ and the other, which contradicts convexity (a vertex of a convex polygon cannot lie inside the triangle of three other vertices). So at most $7$ diagonals can be equal.

**Answer: 7**

hmmt-feb-2014-team-08.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2014-team-08.body:
Put $B=(0,0)$, $C=(6,0)$. From $AB=4$, $AC=5$: $A=\left(\frac94,\frac{5\sqrt7}4\right)$, so $D=\left(\frac94,0\right)$. The area is $\frac{15\sqrt7}4$, so $R=\frac{4\cdot5\cdot6}{4\cdot\frac{15\sqrt7}4}=\frac8{\sqrt7}$, and the circumcenter is $O=\left(3,\frac1{\sqrt7}\right)$ (from $9+y^2=R^2$, with $O$ above $BC$ as the triangle is acute). The line $AO$ meets $BC$ at $E=\left(\frac{96}{31},0\right)$.

Let $X=(x,0)$. Then $Y=\left(\frac94,y\right)$ on $AD$ with $XY\parallel AO$; since $\overrightarrow{AO}=\left(\frac34,-\frac{31}{4\sqrt7}\right)$, we get $y=\frac{31}{3\sqrt7}\left(x-\frac94\right)$.

The condition $YO\perp AX$ reads $\overrightarrow{YO}\cdot\overrightarrow{AX}=0$ with $\overrightarrow{YO}=\left(\frac34,\frac1{\sqrt7}-y\right)$ and $\overrightarrow{AX}=\left(x-\frac94,-\frac{5\sqrt7}4\right)$:
$$\frac34\left(x-\frac94\right)-\frac{5\sqrt7}4\left(\frac1{\sqrt7}-y\right)=0\iff\frac34\left(x-\frac94\right)-\frac54+\frac{155}{12}\left(x-\frac94\right)=0 .$$
So $\frac{41}3\left(x-\frac94\right)=\frac54$, $x-\frac94=\frac{15}{164}$, $x=\frac{384}{164}=\frac{96}{41}$. This lies between $D$ ($2.25$) and $E$ ($\approx3.10$), as required. So $BX=\frac{96}{41}$.

**Answer: $\frac{96}{41}$**

hmmt-feb-2014-team-08.title: Symmedian
hmmt-feb-2014-team-08.body:
Let $AX$ meet the circumcircle again at $K$, and let $OY$ meet $AK$ at $T$ and $BC$ at $L$. Angle chasing with $XY\parallel AO$ and $YO\perp AX$ gives that $LA$ is tangent to the circumcircle and $OL\perp AK$, so $LA=LK$ and $LK$ is tangent too. Thus $L=BC\cap$ (tangents at $A$ and $K$), which means $AK$ is a symmedian of $\triangle ABC$, and so $\frac{BX}{XC}=\frac{AB^2}{AC^2}=\frac{16}{25}$. Hence $BX=\frac{16}{41}\cdot6=\frac{96}{41}$.

**Answer: $\frac{96}{41}$**

hmmt-feb-2014-team-09.title: Replace each entry by its occurrence number
hmmt-feb-2014-team-09.body:
For a valid sequence $a=(a_1,\dots,a_{nm})$ for $(n,m)$ define $f(a)=(b_1,\dots,b_{nm})$, where $b_i$ is the number of $j\le i$ with $a_j=a_i$ (so the $k$-th occurrence of each value is replaced by $k$). For example, $f(1,1,2,1,2,2,1,2,1,2)=(1,2,1,3,2,3,4,4,5,5)$.

*Property (a) with $n,m$ swapped.* Each pair $(\ell,k)$ with $1\le\ell\le n$, $1\le k\le m$ occurs as $(a_i,b_i)$ for exactly one index $i$ (the $k$-th occurrence of $\ell$). So each $k\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ occurs exactly $n$ times in $b$.

*Property (b) with $n,m$ swapped.* Fix $i$. The number of times $k$ appears in $(b_1,\dots,b_i)$ equals the number of values $\ell$ occurring at least $k$ times in $(a_1,\dots,a_i)$ (each such $\ell$ contributes one $k$, at its $k$-th occurrence). For $j\le k$ this number for $j$ is at least that for $k$, so $j$ occurs in $(b_1,\dots,b_i)$ at least as often as $k$.

*$f$ is an involution.* Fix $i$, let $\ell=a_i$ and $k=b_i$, so $\ell$ occurs exactly $k$ times in $(a_1,\dots,a_i)$ and $k-1$ times in $(a_1,\dots,a_{i-1})$. By property (b) at length $i$, every $j\le\ell$ occurs at least $k$ times in $(a_1,\dots,a_i)$. By property (b) at length $i-1$, every $j>\ell$ occurs at most $k-1$ times in $(a_1,\dots,a_{i-1})$, hence at most $k-1$ times in $(a_1,\dots,a_i)$ (as $a_i=\ell\ne j$). So exactly $\ell$ values occur at least $k$ times in $(a_1,\dots,a_i)$, which says the $i$-th term of $f(f(a))$ is $\ell=a_i$. Thus $f(f(a))=a$.

Therefore $f$ is a bijection between the sequences counted by $A(n,m)$ and those counted by $A(m,n)$, and $A(n,m)=A(m,n)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2014-team-09.title: Young tableaux
hmmt-feb-2014-team-09.body: Given a valid sequence, build an $n\times m$ array: when the value $k$ appears, write the next number $i$ (the position in the sequence) into the leftmost empty cell of row $k$. Rows increase left to right, and by property (b) row $k$ always contains at most as many entries as row $k-1$, so columns increase downward: this is a standard Young tableau. The map is reversible (read off the row index of $1,2,\dots,nm$), so $A(n,m)$ equals the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $n\times m$. Transposition is a bijection between $n\times m$ and $m\times n$ tableaux, hence $A(n,m)=A(m,n)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2014-team-10.title: Hölder and a monovariant
hmmt-feb-2014-team-10.body:
Note $L>1$ and $c=\phi^{L-1}$, so $c^{1/(L-1)}=\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}+\phi^{-2}=1$.

**Lemma.** For all $x,y\ge0$: $cx^L+c^2y^L\ge(x+y)^L$.

*Proof.* Apply Hölder's inequality with exponents $L$ and $q=\frac L{L-1}$ to $u=(c^{1/L}x,\;c^{2/L}y)$ and $v=(c^{-1/L},\;c^{-2/L})$:
$$x+y=\sum u_iv_i\le\left(cx^L+c^2y^L\right)^{1/L}\left(c^{-1/(L-1)}+c^{-2/(L-1)}\right)^{(L-1)/L}=\left(cx^L+c^2y^L\right)^{1/L}\left(\phi^{-1}+\phi^{-2}\right)^{(L-1)/L}.$$
Since $\phi^{-1}+\phi^{-2}=1$, raising to the $L$-th power gives the claim. $\square$

**Monovariant.** Put $a=x^L$, $b=y^L$ in the lemma: $(ca+c^2b)^{1/L}\ge a^{1/L}+b^{1/L}$. So when Bob replaces $a,b$ by $ca+c^2b$, the quantity $S=\sum N^{1/L}$ over the numbers $N$ on the board does not decrease.

Initially $S=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left(c^{i}\right)^{1/L}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left(c^{1/L}\right)^i=\frac{c^{n/L}-1}{c^{1/L}-1}$. After $n-1$ minutes a single number $N$ remains, with $N^{1/L}=S_{\text{final}}\ge S_{\text{initial}}$, so $N\ge\left(\frac{c^{n/L}-1}{c^{1/L}-1}\right)^L$. ∎
